extracted.intended_audience: general readers, students, and professionals interested in television technology, broadcast standards, and history
extracted.subtask_description: Summarize technical, regulatory, and format standards and historical decisions affecting television (color encoding, analog→digital transition, scanning formats, broadcast licensing, satellite and display standards). Useful for understanding how and why particular broadcast and display standards were adopted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Color broadcasting compatibility and bandwidth conservation
rubrics_metrics.description: The adopted U.S. color system encoded the color information separately from the brightness information and significantly reduced the resolution of the color information to conserve bandwidth so that black-and-white televisions could receive the same transmission and display it in black-and-white (i.e., 'compatible color').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Brightness image remained compatible with existing B&W sets at slightly reduced resolution; color televisions decode the extra information to produce a limited-resolution color display. Reducing color resolution conserved spectrum and allowed backward compatibility (example: RCA's 'Compatible Color').

rubrics_metrics.name: ATV (Advanced Television) FCC requirement: genuine HDTV
rubrics_metrics.description: In March 1990 the FCC declared the new ATV standard must be more than an enhanced analog signal and be able to provide a genuine HDTV signal with at least twice the resolution of existing television images.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This requirement was intended to ensure a meaningful quality leap over legacy analog systems rather than incremental improvements.

rubrics_metrics.name: ATV simulcast requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: The FCC dictated that the new ATV standard must be capable of being 'simulcast' on different channels so viewers who did not wish to buy a new digital television set could continue to receive conventional television broadcasts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Simulcasting ensured continuity of service during transition and protected viewers without digital-capable sets.

rubrics_metrics.name: No single mandatory scanning/aspect/line standard
rubrics_metrics.description: The FCC's final ATV standards did not require a single standard for scanning formats, aspect ratios, or lines of resolution—a compromise resulting from industry disputes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This flexibility reflected competing industry preferences (consumer electronics/broadcasters vs. computer/film industries) and allowed multiple design approaches to coexist.

rubrics_metrics.name: Suitability of interlaced scanning (pros/cons)
rubrics_metrics.description: Interlaced scanning (scans even-numbered lines first, then odd) was designed for CRTs to double perceived resolution within bandwidth limits and to limit flicker on early CRTs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pros: efficient for transmitting high-line-count pictures (e.g., 1080 lines), compatible with broadcasters' archives. Cons: less efficient on newer displays (LCD) and can produce flicker on non-CRT devices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Suitability of progressive scanning (pros/cons)
rubrics_metrics.description: Progressive scanning scans every line in sequence from top to bottom, producing each full screen in one pass (e.g., 1/60s) and generating more data per full frame than interlaced formats.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pros: avoids flicker on modern displays, easier conversion from film, better suited for Internet connections and progressive-display devices. Industry advocates included the computer and film industries.

rubrics_metrics.name: Digital TV compression prerequisite (DCT)
rubrics_metrics.description: Digital television was previously impractical due to the impractically high bandwidth requirements of uncompressed digital video (around 200 Mbit/s for SDTV and over 1 Gbit/s for HDTV); adoption became practical after the adoption of DCT video compression technology.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: DCT compression enabled feasible digital transmission and was a key technical enabler persuading regulators (e.g., FCC) to consider digital ATV standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Digital multiplexing and program capacity
rubrics_metrics.description: Due to digital processing and multiplexing, digital television can support more than one program on the same channel bandwidth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Multiplexing enabled new services (multiple programs per channel), contributed to the rationale for digital transition, and underpins features like on-demand and additional subchannels.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regulatory licensing and public-service obligations for terrestrial broadcasters
rubrics_metrics.description: Terrestrial television stations are licensed by governments to broadcast over assigned channels; historically (U.S.) the FCC allowed stations to broadcast advertisements beginning July 1941 but required public-service programming commitments as a requirement for a license, while the U.K. funded the BBC via a television license fee to support public service broadcasting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Limited bandwidth (few channels) made government regulation and conditions on licenses common; licensing terms can include commercial allowances and public-service obligations or alternative funding models (license fee).

rubrics_metrics.name: Direct-Broadcast Satellite (DBS/DBSTV) transmission standard
rubrics_metrics.description: In DBSTV systems signals are relayed from a direct broadcast satellite on the Ku wavelength and are completely digital; signals are received via a satellite dish and a low-noise block downconverter (LNB) and decoded by a receiver (set-top box or built-in tuner).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contrast with earlier large 'C-band' analog 'big dish' systems; digital DBS enables wide channel selection, HDTV support, and subscription/pay-TV models as well as free-to-air channels.

rubrics_metrics.name: Display resolution definitions for HD and Ultra HD
rubrics_metrics.description: High-definition television formats include specific defined resolutions (e.g., 1080p 1920×1080, 1080i 1920×1080 interlaced, 720p 1280×720). Ultra-high-definition (Ultra HD) includes 4K (2160p) and 8K (4320p); the CEA specified Ultra HD for displays of at least 16:9 aspect ratio and at least 3840×2160 pixels.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pixel counts and aspect ratios are used to classify display/format capabilities; these definitions underpin marketing, standards, and compatibility decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Digital television transition policy deadlines and adoption dynamics
rubrics_metrics.description: Governments worldwide set deadlines for analog shutdown by the 2010s; initial adoption of digital was low because first digital-tuner-equipped sets were costly, but as prices dropped the transition accelerated and was expected to be completed by the mid-to-late 2010s.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Policy deadlines, cost of consumer equipment, and market price declines are key factors in the pace of digital switchover.

rubrics_metrics.name: Smart TV definition and distinction from Internet/IPTV/Web TV
rubrics_metrics.description: A smart television (connected TV or hybrid TV) is a television set or set-top box with integrated Internet and Web 2.0 features and an operating system; it is distinct from Internet television (distribution over the Internet), IPTV (Internet Protocol television standards), and Web TV (programs created for Internet broadcast).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Smart TVs typically come pre-loaded with an OS, can provide streaming and on-demand services, and may automatically download software routines on demand; manufacturers initially targeted middle/high-end sets and later expanded to broader price points.
